title: Class 6 Maths Perimeter and Area Made Simple (with Case Studies + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Perimeter and Area Explained
meta_desc: Understand class 6 maths perimeter and area the NCERT way: rectangle, square and irregular shapes, plus solved case studies and a free quiz.
excerpt: Perimeter is the fence around a field; area is the grass inside it. Here is the whole NCERT Class 6 mensuration chapter in plain language, with two solved real-life case studies and an 8-question quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The quickest way I have found to fix class 6 maths perimeter and area in a child’s head is a cricket ground. The boundary rope you run around the edge? That length is the perimeter. The green grass the fielders stand on? That is the area. Same ground, two different questions — one about the border, one about the surface — and almost every mistake in this chapter comes from mixing the two up. Get the picture right and the formulas stop feeling like things to memorise.

The NCERT Class 6 mensuration chapter builds in a sensible order: perimeter first (because you can literally walk it), then area, then the awkward shapes that do not fit a neat formula. I will follow that same order here, then solve two real case studies of the kind the chapter loves to ask.

Perimeter: the distance all the way around

Perimeter is just the total length of the boundary. Add up every side. That is the whole idea, and it works for any shape at all — a scribble, a leaf outline, a classroom floor.

For the tidy shapes, though, the adding-up shortcuts into a formula:

  • Rectangle: two lengths and two breadths, so Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth).
  • Square: all four sides equal, so Perimeter = 4 × side.
  • Regular shapes (all sides equal): Perimeter = number of sides × length of one side. A regular hexagon of side 5 cm has a perimeter of 6 × 5 = 30 cm.

A tiny warning that trips up half the class: perimeter is a length, so the answer is in cm or m — never square units. Save the ‘square’ for area.

Area of a rectangle and a square

Area measures the surface a shape covers, counted in unit squares. For a rectangle you do not count them one by one; you multiply.

  • Rectangle: Area = length × breadth.
  • Square: Area = side × side.

Why multiplication? Picture a floor that is 5 tiles long and 3 tiles deep. That is 3 rows of 5 tiles, which is 15 tiles — and 5 × 3 = 15. The formula is just a fast way of counting the rows. I always draw the grid once before writing length × breadth, because a child who sees the rows never forgets why the answer is in square units.

Area by counting squares for irregular shapes

Leaves, footprints, the map of a district — these have no formula. NCERT’s honest method is to put the shape on squared paper and count. The rules the chapter sets are worth learning by heart:

  • A fully covered square counts as 1.
  • More than half covered counts as 1.
  • Exactly half counts as ½.
  • Less than half is ignored.

Add those up and you get a sensible estimate. It will not be exact, and that is the point — this method teaches that area is a measurement, not always a neat whole number.

Compound figures: cut, solve, add

A compound (composite) figure is two or three rectangles stuck together — think of an L-shaped verandah or a plus-shaped garden bed. There is no single formula, and you do not need one. Split the shape into rectangles with a pencil line, find each area separately, then add. For perimeter, ignore the cutting lines and just trace the true outside boundary.

Case study 1: fencing and grassing a garden

A rectangular garden is 20 m long and 12 m wide. A family wants to fence the boundary and lay grass inside.

QuestionFormula usedWorkingAnswer
Length of fence neededPerimeter of rectangle2 × (20 + 12) = 2 × 3264 m
Fencing cost at ₹50 per metrePerimeter × rate64 × 50₹3,200
Grass area requiredArea of rectangle20 × 12240 sq m
Grass cost at ₹15 per sq mArea × rate240 × 15₹3,600

Notice how the case study forces the child to choose: fencing is a boundary job, so it needs perimeter; grass covers the surface, so it needs area. That choosing step is the real skill the exam is testing, far more than the arithmetic.

Case study 2: a passage of floor tiles

A rectangular passage is 8 m long and 3 m wide, to be covered with square tiles of side 1 m. How many tiles, and what does the border skirting cost?

Area of the passage = 8 × 3 = 24 sq m. Each tile covers 1 sq m, so 24 tiles are needed. For skirting along the boundary, use the perimeter: 2 × (8 + 3) = 22 m. At ₹40 per metre, the skirting costs 22 × 40 = ₹880. One passage, both ideas, no confusion — because you asked ‘surface or border?’ before reaching for a formula.

Common slips to watch for

  • Writing the perimeter answer in square units, or the area in plain metres.
  • Using length × breadth for a square instead of side × side (both work, but only if you use the right numbers).
  • Forgetting to convert — every measurement must be in the same unit before you calculate.

Try the quiz, then the solved case studies

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly this chapter — perimeter, area, counting squares and a word problem or two. Let your child attempt it and read each explanation. When they are ready for exam-style practice, the printable case-study e-book at the end walks through many more garden, floor and field problems with full step-by-step solutions.

quiz.title: Class 6 Perimeter and Area Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on perimeter, area, counting squares and real-life word problems. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 15 cm long and 5 cm wide?
The perimeter of a square is 4 × side. What is the perimeter of a square of side 9 cm?
questions.explanation: 4 × 9 = 36 cm. (81 would be the area, side × side.)

questions.q: What is the area of a rectangle 12 m long and 4 m wide?
A square field has side 7 m. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a square = side × side = 7 × 7 = 49 sq m.

questions.q: On squared paper, how much does a square that is exactly half covered count as?
questions.explanation: NCERT rule: exactly half covered counts as ½; more than half counts as 1; less than half is ignored.

questions.q: A regular pentagon has each side 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: A pentagon has 5 equal sides, so perimeter = 5 × 6 = 30 cm.

questions.q: A garden is 25 m by 10 m. How much wire is needed to fence its boundary once?
A floor 6 m by 4 m is tiled with square tiles of side 1 m. How many tiles are needed?
questions.explanation: Number of tiles = area of floor = 6 × 4 = 24 sq m, and each tile covers 1 sq m, so 24 tiles.

faq.q: What is the difference between perimeter and area in Class 6?
faq.a: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a shape, measured in units like cm or m. Area is the surface the shape covers, measured in square units like sq cm or sq m. A fence uses perimeter; grass or tiles use area.

faq.q: What are the perimeter and area formulas I must remember for Class 6?
faq.a: Just four: perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + breadth); perimeter of a square = 4 × side; area of a rectangle = length × breadth; area of a square = side × side. Everything else in the chapter is built from these.

faq.q: How do you find the area of an irregular shape like a leaf?
faq.a: Place it on squared paper and count. A fully covered square is 1, more than half is 1, exactly half is ½, and less than half is ignored. Adding these gives a good estimate — it will not be perfectly exact, and that is expected.

faq.q: How do you solve a compound or L-shaped figure?
faq.a: For area, split it into rectangles, find each area, and add them. For perimeter, ignore the cutting lines and trace the true outer boundary all the way around. Never add the internal lines to the perimeter.
